warmup.q: On a table of 1,000,000 payments with a primary key on payment_id, how does PostgreSQL 18 run WITH p AS (SELECT * FROM payments) SELECT * FROM p WHERE payment_id = 42?
options: It copies all 1,000,000 rows into a temporary result, then searches the copy for id 42
It looks up id 42 in the primary key index, as if the CTE were not there
It raises an error: a CTE cannot be filtered from outside
It runs the CTE once per row of the outer query
warmup.why: Since PostgreSQL 12, a CTE that is referenced once, is not recursive and has no side effects is inlined: pasted into the main query and planned with it, so the filter reaches the index. The copy-everything behaviour is what older versions did, and what MATERIALIZED still asks for. It is the old "optimization fence" advice, which is out of date.

sections.h: A subquery is a query in a place that wants a value
sections.html:
"Payments above the average payment" is a two-step question: find the average, then compare each payment with it. From the application that is two round trips. You run SELECT avg(amount_minor) ..., read 24015.17 into a Kotlin variable, and send a second query with that number bound as a parameter. Between the two, another transaction can insert payments and move the average, and you have written glue code for something the database can do in one statement.

Put the first query inside the second, in parentheses, where the number would go:

SELECT payment_id, merchant_id, amount_minor
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'succeeded'
  AND amount_minor > (SELECT avg(amount_minor) FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded');

A query in parentheses inside another statement is a subquery. PostgreSQL computes it and uses its result in that spot, and this one returns the nine payments above 24,015.17. The picture for this lesson is simple: a subquery is a query used as a value, and the shape of its result decides where it may go. There are three shapes.

One column and at most one row is a scalar subquery. It can go anywhere a single value can: in WHERE, in the SELECT list, inside an expression. If it returns no row, its value is NULL. If it returns two rows, the statement fails with more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression. PostgreSQL checks this while the query runs, on the rows that exist that day, so a scalar subquery that works on test data can fail in production the day a customer gets a second card.

One column and many rows is a list. It goes after IN, = ANY or <> ALL, or inside EXISTS, which lesson 3 used for semi and anti joins. card_id IN (SELECT card_id FROM cards WHERE brand = 'amex') keeps the payments made with any amex card. Write = instead of IN and the query fails, because two cards are amex.

Several columns and many rows is a table. It goes in FROM, where it is called a derived table. Lesson 4 used one to fold refunds per payment before joining them. PostgreSQL required an alias on a derived table until version 16; give it one anyway, so the rest of the query can name its columns.

None of these subqueries mention the outer query. PostgreSQL notices that and runs each one once, before the outer query needs its value. EXPLAIN calls such a subquery an InitPlan: a plan that runs once, at initialization.

try.title: Three shapes of subquery
steps: Start the database if it is not running (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait, from the labs folder) and open psql: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course.
Run the first two queries: a scalar subquery and a list subquery.
Run the third, which uses = where the second used IN, and read the error. Then run the fourth, whose subquery finds no row.
Run the EXPLAIN and find the InitPlan: the average is computed once, before the scan.

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: \pset null '∅' SELECT payment_id, merchant_id, amount_minor FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded' AND amount_minor > (SELECT avg(amount_minor) FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded') ORDER BY amount_minor DESC; SELECT payment_id, card_id, amount_minor FROM payments WHERE card_id IN (SELECT card_id FROM cards WHERE brand = 'amex') ORDER BY payment_id; SELECT payment_id FROM payments WHERE card_id = (SELECT card_id FROM cards WHERE brand = 'amex'); SELECT (SELECT card_id FROM cards WHERE pan_last4 = '0000') AS card; EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) SELECT payment_id FROM payments WHERE amount_minor > (SELECT avg(amount_minor) FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded');

try.expect:
The first query returns nine payments, from 3 (129900) down to 16 (31500): all of them at merchants 4 and 5. The IN query returns payments 4, 10, 19 and 30, made with amex cards 4 and 10. The = version fails with ERROR: more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression. The empty scalar subquery returns one row with card shown as ∅: no row means NULL. The plan:

                       QUERY PLAN
---------------------------------------------------------
 Seq Scan on payments
   Filter: ((amount_minor)::numeric > (InitPlan 1).col1)
   InitPlan 1
     ->  Aggregate
           ->  Seq Scan on payments payments_1
                 Filter: (status = 'succeeded'::text)
(6 rows)

(InitPlan 1).col1 is the one value the InitPlan computed, used by the filter on every row.

sections.h: A correlated subquery runs again for every outer row
sections.html:
Risk does not want payments above the global average. A 550-cent payment is tiny for Volt Electronics and twice the usual fare at Metro Transit, whose rides cost 275. The question is "larger than this merchant's average", and now the subquery needs a value from the row being tested:

SELECT p.payment_id, p.merchant_id, p.amount_minor
FROM payments p
WHERE p.status = 'succeeded'
  AND p.amount_minor > (SELECT avg(p2.amount_minor)
                        FROM payments p2
                        WHERE p2.status = 'succeeded'
                          AND p2.merchant_id = p.merchant_id);   -- the outer row's merchant

p.merchant_id belongs to the outer query. A subquery that refers to the outer query is correlated: it is a function of the outer row. In lesson 3's loop picture it runs once for every outer row, with that row's values plugged in, as the stepper below shows. EXPLAIN gives it a different name: a correlated subquery appears as a SubPlan, run on demand for each row that needs it.

Aliases matter more here than anywhere else in SQL. A column name inside a subquery is looked up in the subquery's own FROM first, and in the outer query only if that fails. Write WHERE merchant_id = merchant_id and both names find the inner payments. The condition is then true for every row, the subquery is no longer correlated, and the query quietly compares every payment with the global average again. The lab starts with exactly this bug. Qualify every column in a correlated subquery.

Running once per outer row costs what it sounds like. On the large data set, each run of this subquery scans a million payments to find one merchant's rows, which takes about 51 ms. For the first 20 payments that adds up to 1.1 seconds. For all 930,826 succeeded payments it would be about 13 hours. The same question written as a join takes 282 ms: one pass computes the 2,500 merchant averages with GROUP BY, and a hash join (lesson 3) attaches each payment to its merchant's average.

SELECT p.payment_id, p.merchant_id, p.amount_minor
FROM payments p
JOIN (SELECT merchant_id, avg(amount_minor) AS avg_minor
      FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded'
      GROUP BY merchant_id) a ON a.merchant_id = p.merchant_id
WHERE p.status = 'succeeded' AND p.amount_minor > a.avg_minor;

Correlated subqueries are not always slow. PostgreSQL rewrites some of them into joins on its own: EXISTS, NOT EXISTS and IN (subquery) become semi and anti joins, which is why lesson 3's NOT EXISTS plan showed a Hash Anti Join and no SubPlan. PostgreSQL 18 does not rewrite a subquery that computes an aggregate, like the average here. And a correlated subquery that finds its rows through an index (lesson 1's B-tree; the Storage track covers indexes properly) costs a few page reads per run, which is fine when the outer side is small. Read the plan: a SubPlan whose loops count matches a big table is the thing to rewrite.

video.title: A correlated subquery runs once per row

sections.h: WITH gives a subquery a name
sections.html:
Subqueries nest, and nested queries read from the inside out. Here is each merchant's share of all succeeded volume, written with a derived table and a scalar subquery:

SELECT v.merchant_id, v.volume,
       round(100.0 * v.volume / (SELECT sum(amount_minor) FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded'), 1) AS pct
FROM (SELECT merchant_id, sum(amount_minor) AS volume
      FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded'
      GROUP BY merchant_id) AS v;

To read it you start in the middle at the derived table, jump to the scalar subquery, and come back out. The two inner queries also say the same thing twice, "succeeded payments, summed", and when one of them changes the other has to change with it.

A common table expression, or CTE, names a subquery before the main query: WITH name AS (query). Inside that one statement, the name works like a table:

WITH volume AS (                    -- succeeded volume per merchant
    SELECT merchant_id, sum(amount_minor) AS volume
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'succeeded'
    GROUP BY merchant_id
),
total AS (                          -- a CTE may use the CTEs above it
    SELECT sum(volume) AS total FROM volume
)
SELECT v.merchant_id, v.volume, round(100.0 * v.volume / t.total, 1) AS pct
FROM volume v
CROSS JOIN total t;                 -- total has one row: attach it to every merchant

It reads top to bottom, like val declarations in a Kotlin function. Each step has a name, and a later step can use any earlier one. total is computed from volume, so "succeeded" is defined in one place. The answer is the same six rows: Volt Electronics has 47.2% of the volume and Harbor Hotel 46.6%. The last line uses lesson 3's cross join, every row paired with every row: with a one-row table on one side, that attaches the total to each merchant.

A CTE exists only for its own statement. It is not a temporary table and not a view: the next statement cannot see it, and nothing is stored anywhere. Several CTEs go in one WITH, separated by commas, and they can be used by the main query as often as you like.

For a plain SELECT, a CTE does not let you ask anything a derived table cannot. The exceptions are recursion (WITH RECURSIVE, which the Data models track uses for trees and graphs) and CTEs that change data, at the end of the next section. What a CTE changes is how the query reads. It can also change how PostgreSQL runs it, which is the subject of the next section.

try.title: Name the steps
steps: Run the nested version and the CTE version. Check that they return the same rows.

Add a third CTE after total, big AS (SELECT merchant_id FROM volume v, total t WHERE v.volume > t.total / 10), and change the main query to list only merchants in big. Predict how many rows come back.

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: SELECT v.merchant_id, v.volume, round(100.0 * v.volume / (SELECT sum(amount_minor) FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded'), 1) AS pct FROM (SELECT merchant_id, sum(amount_minor) AS volume FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded' GROUP BY merchant_id) AS v ORDER BY v.volume DESC; WITH volume AS ( SELECT merchant_id, sum(amount_minor) AS volume FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded' GROUP BY merchant_id ), total AS ( SELECT sum(volume) AS total FROM volume ) SELECT v.merchant_id, v.volume, round(100.0 * v.volume / t.total, 1) AS pct FROM volume v CROSS JOIN total t ORDER BY v.volume DESC;

Both return:

-------------+--------+------

(6 rows)

With the big CTE, two merchants are left: 4 and 5. Everyone else has less than a tenth of the volume.

sections.h: PostgreSQL pastes a CTE into the query unless you ask it not to
sections.html:
Older advice says a CTE is an "optimization fence". Until PostgreSQL 12 that was true. PostgreSQL computed every CTE completely, stored its rows, and ran the main query against the stored copy, so a filter in the main query could not reach the table inside the CTE, and neither could that table's indexes. The keyword MATERIALIZED still asks for that behaviour, and on the large data set you can see what it costs:

WITH succeeded AS MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT payment_id, merchant_id, amount_minor FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded'
)
SELECT * FROM succeeded WHERE payment_id = 424242;

PostgreSQL scans all million payments, writes the 930,826 succeeded ones to a temporary store (30 MB, spilled to disk), then searches the copy for one id: 214 ms. Remove the keyword, and the plan becomes a single Index Scan using payments_pkey: 0.24 ms, almost a thousand times faster.

Since version 12, PostgreSQL inlines a CTE when three things are true: it is not recursive, it has no side effects (a plain SELECT with no volatile function such as random()), and the main query refers to it once. Inlining means pasting the CTE's query into the main query, as if you had written a derived table, and then planning the whole statement together. That is how the payment_id = 424242 filter reached the primary key index.

A CTE referenced two or more times, by the main query or by other CTEs, is materialized by default: computed once, stored, and read by every reference. Often that is cheaper than computing it twice. In the share-of-volume query from the last section, volume is used twice and materialized, while total is used once and inlined; the Try it shows both in one plan. Materializing also hides the main query's filters from the CTE, though. A query that joined succeeded to itself and filtered on one id took 318 ms on the large data set; with NOT MATERIALIZED, which forces inlining, it took 0.08 ms.

So the two keywords are overrides for the planner's default. NOT MATERIALIZED asks PostgreSQL to inline even when it would not. MATERIALIZED asks it to compute once, which pays off when the CTE is expensive and inlining would run it many times, or when it calls a volatile function that must run only once. Write neither by default. Reach for one when EXPLAIN shows a CTE Scan reading far more rows than the query returns, or the same expensive work done twice.

Two kinds of CTE are never inlined. A recursive CTE, the Data models track's tool for walking trees and graphs, is always computed on its own. And a CTE that changes data, such as WITH moved AS (DELETE FROM jobs WHERE status = 'done' RETURNING *), runs exactly once and to completion, whether or not the main query reads its rows.

try.title: Inlined or materialized?
steps: On the small data (SET search_path = public; if you changed it), EXPLAIN the share-of-volume query. Find which CTE has its own CTE volume node and which one disappeared into the plan.
On the large data set (SET search_path = big, public;), run the two EXPLAIN ANALYZE statements. They differ in one keyword.
When you are done with the large data set, DROP SCHEMA big CASCADE; frees the space, or keep it: lessons 6 to 9 use it again.

code.title: psql, database course
code.html: SET search_path = public; EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) WITH volume AS ( SELECT merchant_id, sum(amount_minor) AS volume FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded' GROUP BY merchant_id ), total AS (SELECT sum(volume) AS total FROM volume) SELECT v.merchant_id, v.volume, round(100.0 * v.volume / t.total, 1) AS pct FROM volume v CROSS JOIN total t; SET search_path = big, public; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, BUFFERS OFF) WITH succeeded AS ( SELECT payment_id, merchant_id, amount_minor FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded' ) SELECT * FROM succeeded WHERE payment_id = 424242; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, BUFFERS OFF) WITH succeeded AS MATERIALIZED ( SELECT payment_id, merchant_id, amount_minor FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded' ) SELECT * FROM succeeded WHERE payment_id = 424242;

try.expect:
The small plan has a CTE volume node and two CTE Scan on volume nodes, because volume is referenced twice. total has no node of its own: it was inlined into an Aggregate over one of those scans. On the large data set the inlined CTE is just an index lookup:

 Index Scan using payments_pkey on payments (actual time=0.211..0.214 rows=1.00 loops=1)
   Index Cond: (payment_id = 424242)
   Filter: (status = 'succeeded'::text)
   Index Searches: 1
 Planning Time: 0.327 ms
 Execution Time: 0.243 ms

The materialized one builds the whole copy first:

 CTE Scan on succeeded (actual time=92.542..212.188 rows=1.00 loops=1)
   Filter: (payment_id = 424242)
   Rows Removed by Filter: 930825
   Storage: Disk  Maximum Storage: 30904kB
   CTE succeeded
     ->  Seq Scan on payments (actual time=0.123..89.939 rows=930826.00 loops=1)
           Filter: (status = 'succeeded'::text)
           Rows Removed by Filter: 69652
 Planning Time: 0.061 ms
 Execution Time: 213.792 ms

The answer is the same row. Only the work differs.

analogy: A CTE is a named step in a recipe: "make the stock", then "use one cup of stock in the soup". A cook who inlines reads the whole recipe first and makes only the cup the soup needs. A cook who materializes makes a full pot of stock first and then ladles out one cup, which is worth it when three dishes use the stock and wasteful when one does. A correlated subquery is the instruction "for each guest, taste the sauce at their table": you walk back to the pot once per guest, even when two guests share a table. The analogy breaks at the result. Two cooks can make different soups, but PostgreSQL returns the same rows whether it inlines or materializes (volatile functions such as random() aside), so the choice is only about speed.
world: A lot of slow reporting SQL in payments services is a correlated aggregate written for clarity: "each merchant with its last payment time", "each card with its average risk score", as a scalar subquery in the SELECT list. It was fast on staging with 5,000 rows and turns into a SubPlan with a million loops in production. The same thing happens one level up when JPA lazy loading runs one query per entity (the N+1 problem of lesson 10). CTEs earn their keep in the long queries a settlement or reconciliation job runs: name each step, check each step on its own with SELECT * FROM step, then build on it. If your team still writes CTE-free SQL because of the "optimization fence" advice, that advice died with PostgreSQL 12. And a data-modifying CTE gives a Temporal activity or a Kafka consumer a way to move rows atomically in one statement: delete from the outbox and insert into the sent log, with no window between the two.
mistake: The most damaging subquery mistake is an unqualified column that resolves to the wrong table. Inside a subquery, a name is looked up in the subquery's own FROM first and then in the outer query, and PostgreSQL raises no error either way. merchant_id = merchant_id compares the inner table with itself and is always true. Worse, if the inner table has no such column, the name silently binds to the outer one: SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM merchants) returns 13, all customers, because merchants has no customer_id and the subquery returns the outer row's own id once per merchant. Put that pattern in a DELETE and it deletes every row. Always alias every table in a statement with a subquery and qualify every column: SELECT m.customer_id FROM merchants m fails with column m.customer_id does not exist, which is the error you wanted.

compare.title: Moving rows in one statement: Oracle and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle
a.html: -- WITH holds queries only: no DML inside it. -- Archive, then delete, as two statements: INSERT INTO jobs_archive SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE status = 'done'; DELETE FROM jobs WHERE status = 'done'; COMMIT; -- each statement takes its own snapshot: a job -- that turns 'done' in between is deleted -- without being archived. Close the gap with a -- lock, or PL/SQL DELETE ... RETURNING BULK COLLECT.

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18
b.html: -- a data-modifying CTE: the rows the DELETE -- returns are exactly the rows inserted WITH moved AS ( DELETE FROM jobs WHERE status = 'done' RETURNING * ) INSERT INTO jobs_archive SELECT * FROM moved; -- INSERT 0 2 (jobs 1 and 4) -- runs exactly once, even if nothing reads moved

compare.note: PostgreSQL allows INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE with RETURNING inside WITH, and runs each of them exactly once and to completion. The rows a DELETE removes are the rows the INSERT receives, in one statement and one snapshot, so nothing can slip between them. Oracle's WITH clause holds queries only. Oracle also has no keyword like MATERIALIZED: its SQL reference says the optimizer treats each query name "as either an inline view or as a temporary table", and it chooses. Plain query CTEs, scalar and correlated subqueries, and the name-resolution rule behave the same in both databases.

worked.title: Rewrite a per-row subquery as a join, and prove nothing changed

steps.say: The fraud desk flags payments whose risk score is more than 30 points above the average score of their card. The first version is a correlated subquery. It is correct and easy to read, and on the small data it returns six payments.
steps.code: -- 1. the correlated version: the subquery depends on p.card_id SELECT p.payment_id, p.card_id, (p.metadata->'risk'->>'score')::int AS score FROM payments p WHERE (p.metadata->'risk'->>'score')::int > (SELECT avg((p2.metadata->'risk'->>'score')::int) + 30 FROM payments p2 WHERE p2.card_id = p.card_id) ORDER BY p.payment_id; -- payments 8, 15, 18, 23, 31 and 36

steps.say: Before you change anything, read the plan. SubPlan 1 with p2.card_id = p.card_id inside it means one full scan of payments per outer row. With 100,000 cards and a million payments that is a million scans.
steps.code: -- 2. EXPLAIN (COSTS OFF) of step 1 -- Seq Scan on payments p -- Filter: (((((metadata -> 'risk'::text) ->> 'score'::text))::integer)::numeric > (SubPlan 1)) -- SubPlan 1 -- -> Aggregate -- -> Seq Scan on payments p2 -- Filter: (card_id = p.card_id)

steps.say: Compute what the subquery computes, for every card at once, in a CTE. Then join each payment to its card's row. The extra column shows the average each payment was compared with, which the correlated version could not show without a second subquery.
steps.code: -- 3. averages once, then a join WITH card_risk AS ( SELECT card_id, avg((metadata->'risk'->>'score')::int) AS avg_score FROM payments GROUP BY card_id ) SELECT p.payment_id, p.card_id, (p.metadata->'risk'->>'score')::int AS score, round(c.avg_score, 1) AS card_avg FROM payments p JOIN card_risk c ON c.card_id = p.card_id WHERE (p.metadata->'risk'->>'score')::int > c.avg_score + 30 ORDER BY p.payment_id; -- 8 (67 vs 30.7), 15 (88 vs 52.0), 18 (79 vs 35.3), -- 23 (52 vs 16.4), 31 (72 vs 40.5), 36 (61 vs 17.0)

steps.say: Prove that the rewrite returns the same rows, instead of eyeballing six ids. EXCEPT ALL returns the rows of the first query that the second lacks, duplicates included. Run it in both directions: zero rows means the two results are equal as bags of rows. Keep this check for every refactoring of a report.
steps.code: -- 4. old minus new, plus new minus old: expect (0 rows) WITH old AS ( /* step 1 without ORDER BY, selecting payment_id */ ), new AS ( /* step 3 without ORDER BY, selecting payment_id */ ) (SELECT * FROM old EXCEPT ALL SELECT * FROM new) UNION ALL (SELECT * FROM new EXCEPT ALL SELECT * FROM old);

lab.title: A subquery that only looks correlated, an average at the wrong grain, and a CTE pipeline
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the labs folder. All six fail. Each failure prints the expected rows next to yours.

above_merchant_average.sql compares every payment with the average over all merchants, although it looks correlated. Find which table each merchant_id in the subquery names, then fix it with aliases or with a join to per-merchant averages.
above_average_spenders.sql compares customers' totals with the average payment. Compute spend per customer in a CTE and use it twice.
Write monthly_active_customers.sql as a pipeline of CTEs: (customer, month) pairs, then each customer's first month, then the counts.
Run the tests until all six pass. Each exercise has a second test that adds rows first, so a hard-coded answer fails it.
hints: Run the placeholder's subquery on its own in psql, with merchant_id = merchant_id left in: it returns one number, 24015.17. A correlated subquery cannot run on its own.
The grain of a question is what one row stands for. "Average customer spend" needs one row per customer before avg.

SELECT DISTINCT a.customer_id, to_char(p.created_at, 'YYYY-MM') AS month gives one row per customer and month. 'YYYY-MM' text sorts in time order, so min(month) is the first month, and count(*) FILTER (WHERE ac.month = f.month) counts the new ones.

drill.title: Three subqueries from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write: (1) payments whose amount is above the average succeeded amount, with a scalar subquery; (2) the same for each payment's own card instead, as a correlated subquery with every column qualified; (3) version 2 rewritten with a CTE of per-card averages and a join. Then say what EXPLAIN calls the subquery in (1) and in (2).

answer.html: -- 1. uncorrelated: EXPLAIN shows an InitPlan, run once SELECT payment_id, amount_minor FROM payments WHERE amount_minor > (SELECT avg(amount_minor) FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded'); -- 2. correlated: EXPLAIN shows a SubPlan, run per outer row SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount_minor FROM payments p WHERE p.amount_minor > (SELECT avg(p2.amount_minor) FROM payments p2 WHERE p2.status = 'succeeded' AND p2.card_id = p.card_id); -- 3. the averages once, then a join WITH card_avg AS ( SELECT card_id, avg(amount_minor) AS avg_minor FROM payments WHERE status = 'succeeded' GROUP BY card_id ) SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount_minor FROM payments p JOIN card_avg c ON c.card_id = p.card_id WHERE p.amount_minor > c.avg_minor;

recap: A subquery is a query used as a value. Scalar (one row, one column) goes where a value goes; a column list goes after IN, ANY or EXISTS; a table goes in FROM as a derived table.
A scalar subquery with no row is NULL; with two rows it fails at run time, on whatever data exists that day.
An uncorrelated subquery runs once (InitPlan). A correlated one refers to the outer row and runs per row (SubPlan), unless PostgreSQL turns it into a join, as it does for EXISTS and IN.
Inside a subquery, a column name binds to the nearest table that has it. Qualify every column, or a correlated subquery silently stops being correlated.
WITH names subqueries so a query reads top to bottom. Since PostgreSQL 12 a CTE used once is inlined; one used twice is materialized. MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED override.

explain.prompt: A teammate writes "each merchant with its average payment" as SELECT m.*, (SELECT avg(p.amount_minor) FROM payments p WHERE p.merchant_id = m.merchant_id) FROM merchants m. It is fast with 8 merchants. Explain how PostgreSQL runs it, when it gets slow, and what you would write instead.
explain.answer: The subquery refers to m.merchant_id, so it is correlated: PostgreSQL runs it as a SubPlan once for each merchant, and with no index on payments.merchant_id every run scans the whole payments table. The cost is merchants times payments: fine for 8 merchants and 37 payments, terrible for 2,500 merchants and a million payments, about 2,500 full scans. PostgreSQL does not turn an aggregate subquery into a join by itself. Write the averages once, SELECT merchant_id, avg(amount_minor) FROM payments GROUP BY merchant_id, in a CTE or derived table, and LEFT JOIN merchants to it, so merchants without payments still get a row with NULL. That is two passes over the data. An index on payments (merchant_id) would also make each SubPlan run cheap, but the join is simpler to reason about.

deeper.html:
A data-modifying CTE is worth trying once, inside a transaction you roll back. This one moves the finished jobs to an archive table in one statement:

BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE jobs_archive (LIKE jobs);

WITH moved AS (
    DELETE FROM jobs
    WHERE status = 'done'
    RETURNING *
)
INSERT INTO jobs_archive
SELECT * FROM moved;

SELECT job_id, kind, status FROM jobs_archive ORDER BY job_id;
SELECT count(*) AS left_in_jobs FROM jobs;
ROLLBACK;

The INSERT reports INSERT 0 2. The archive holds jobs 1 (fraud_review) and 4 (send_receipt), both done, and 6 jobs are left in jobs. ROLLBACK puts everything back.

All parts of the statement see the same snapshot of the data, taken when the statement starts. That has a surprising consequence: the main query cannot see the changes its own CTEs make to tables. WITH d AS (DELETE FROM jobs WHERE status = 'done') SELECT count(*) FROM jobs still counts 8, because the SELECT reads the snapshot from before the DELETE. Only the RETURNING rows carry the changes forward. The PostgreSQL docs also warn against changing the same row twice in one statement: which change wins is not predictable.

Subqueries have one more shape worth knowing by name: a row subquery, which returns one row with several columns and compares them all at once. WHERE (card_id, amount_minor) = (SELECT card_id, amount_minor FROM payments WHERE payment_id = 17) finds payments with the same card and amount as payment 17: here 17 and its duplicate 18. Lesson 8 uses the same row comparison, with <, for keyset pagination.

Finally, ANY and ALL with an empty list. x > ALL (empty) is true, because there is no element it fails against, while x > (SELECT max(...) FROM empty) compares with NULL and is never true. The two look interchangeable and part ways exactly when the subquery finds nothing.
